notes.title: “This is My body… this is My blood”
notes.intro: At the Last Supper Jesus gives bread and wine with these words. Christians have understood them in different ways.

views.label: The bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood
views.summary: Catholic and Orthodox Christians take Jesus’ words as making the bread and wine truly his body and blood.
views.source: Catechism of the Catholic Church 1374–1376; Confession of Dositheus, Decree 17

views.label: Christ’s body and blood are present in, with and under the bread and wine
views.summary: Lutherans take the words literally while holding that the bread and wine remain.

views.label: Christ is spiritually present and received by faith
views.summary: Reformed, Anglican and Methodist Christians affirm a real spiritual presence without a change in the elements.

views.label: The bread and wine represent his body and blood
views.summary: Many evangelical churches read “is” as “represents,” and see the meal as a memorial.
views.source: Baptist Faith and Message (2000), Article VII

notes.common: See the Big Question “What happens at Communion?”
